explanation: DNA replication differs structurally between prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Prokaryotes typically have a single circular chromosome, and replication begins at a single site. This initiates two replication forks that move in opposite directions around the circle until the entire DNA molecule is copied. Eukaryotes, however, have long, linear chromosomes containing about 3 billion base pairs of DNA. Because of this massive length, replication would take too long if it started at only one site. Therefore, eukaryotic replication begins at many points along the DNA, known as origins of replication, which occur every few thousand base pairs.

questions.q: How does the number of replication origins differ between prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
opts: Prokaryotes have multiple origins, whereas eukaryotes have only one.
Prokaryotes have one origin, whereas eukaryotes have many origins along their chromosomes.
Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes have only a single origin of replication.
Neither prokaryotes nor eukaryotes use origins of replication.
questions.exp: Option B is correct because the slide states that prokaryotes have replication beginning 'at one place' and eukaryotes have replication beginning 'at many points along DNA.' Option A is the opposite, and Options C and D are incorrect.
